title: "Research Background and Aims"

## Abstract

The classification of fossil populations informs on such evolutionary dynamics as reproductive and behavioral cohesion, adaptation, and patterns of divergence, anagenesis, and reticulation. Species designations therefore provide the individual components from which we articulate our understanding of human evolutionary pattern and process. Determining how these populations should be classified, however, is a daunting task often spurring debate and conflicting interpretation. Here I build on efforts to disentangle variation from diversity in the human fossil record. Such research is of relevance in Late Chibanian paleoanthropology as new designations are being offered and debated for fossils across Africa and Eurasia (e.g., Homo longi, Homo juluensis, and Homo bodoensis). 

This research tackles the broader issue of species delineation while more narrowly investigating Late Chibanian hominin species diversity. It is pursued by implementing 3D Geometric Morphometrics to investigate species boundaries, morphological distance, and phylogenetics. Specifically, species boundaries will be investigated by using a geographically and temporally broad sample of H. sapiens to establish a model range of variation by which fossil populations can be compared. Late Chibanian Chinese fossils which have eluded classification until recently will be considered against this model to determine if and how many different species comprise the assemblage. As there are currently two posited species designations for the assemblage (H. longi and H. juluensis), the rest of the project will focus on testing these taxa. This will be done following the Phylogenetic Species Concept by first running a phylogenetic analysis (using 3DGM and discrete data) of these fossils amidst the greater Chibanian fossil record and subsequently partitioning the clades into species groupings through Principal Components Analysis (PCA). 

## Project Context

The Late Middle Pleistocene (hereafter referred to as the "Chibanian") spans from approximatly 350 Ka to 100 ka 
and is characterized by climate instability, shifting sea
levels, and faunal dispersals which reflect much of today's
modern biota. As it pertains to paleoanthropology, the Chibanian hosts a minimum of three widely agreed 
upon hominin species: *Homo erectus* (~1.8 Ma-125 Ka), *Homo 
neanderthalensis* (~440 ka-30 Ka), and *Homo sapiens* (~300 
Ka-present). In addition to these agreed upon taxa, many scholars 
recognize or argue for the existence of additional hominin species 
designations. These include commonly discussed nomina such as *Homo 
heidelbergensis* and *Homo floresiensis*, as well as lesser understood taxa such as *Homo naledi*, *Homo longi*, and *Homo juluensis* (see Table 1). Further, while *H. 
heidelbergensis* is a commonly referenced taxon, recent 
considerations have divided the assemblage into the already 
well-regarded *H. neanderthalensis* taxon throughout Europe and a 
new designation of *H. bodoensis* in Africa. The latter designation would also encapsulate the contended *H. rhodesiensis* named by Woodward in 1921. 


|      Species           |       Date          |  Region/Country      |
|:----------------------:|:-------------------:|:--------------------:|
| *H. sapiens*           | ~300ka-Present      |    Global            |
| *H. neanderthalensis*  | ~440-30ka           | W. Eurasia           |
| *H. erectus*           | ~1.8Ma-125ka        | Africa/Eurasia       |
| *H. floresiensis*      | ~100-50ka           | S.E. Asia/Indonesia  |
| *`H. heidelbergensis`*| ~600-200ka          | W. Eurasia (see below)|
| *`H. naledi`*         | ~335-236ka          | South Africa         |
| *`H. rhodesiensis`*   |        N/A[^1]      | Zimbabwe             |
| *`H. bodoensis`*       |        N/A[^2]      | Africa/W. Eurasia    |
| *`H. longi`*           | ~309-138ka[^3]      | China                |
| *`H. juluensis`*       |        N/A[^4]      | China                |

[^1]: *H. rhodesiensis* would have ICZN priority for the Kabwe/Broken Hill specimen if were to be removed from the *H. heidelbergensis* designation. Roksandic et al. 2022 challenge this designation on ethical grounds given the nomina's association with Cecil Rhodes and a call to remove taxonomic names with ethical baggage (i.e., racism, colonialism, genocide, and etcetera). As it stands, this designation does not have a known/accepted date range.

[^2]: *H. bodoensis* is the taxonomic designation offered to replace *H. rhodesiensis* an encapsulate specimens such as Bodo, Kabwe, and others. There is no current precedent for such replacement by the current ICZN standards. As such, the ICZN will need to change the rules governing taxonomic designation before this taxon will be accepted. As it stands, this designation does not have a known/accepted date range.

[^3]: This species was named by Ji et al., 2021 but not largely accepted. It encompasses a single speciemen (Harbin) belonging to a larger clade of eastern Asian Chibanian hominins including Dali, Hualongdong, Jinniushan, Xujiayao, and possibly Xiahe (Ni et al., 2021). The date range listed here is based solely on the Harbin specimen. 

[^4]: *H. juluensis* is the designation suggested by Bae 2024 and supported by Wu and Bae 2024 for the Xuchang, Xujiayao, Xiahe, and Penghu specimens. The current date range is not established but, based on this hypodigm should span between ~220-105ka.

Kaifu and Athreya (2024) suggest that the "high level of craniodental variability" observable in the Asian Chibanian fossils has "defied efforts" to classify them along morphological grounds (4). While not directly approaching the subject of how many species are present in this assemblage or where the species boundaries should be drawn, they outline theoretical explanations for where the observed variation might have come from. [*might be getting off track. want to focus on the first statement that there is such a high level of variation that we cannot confidently discern higher level taxa. My initial thought is that there isn't any more variation present in this sample as there is in named (accepted) species. If there is less variation than we have identified in other species (i.e. H. sapiens and H. erectus) then this statement should be challenged and the reasons for taxonomic timidness can be explained in other ways.*] They state that the "lack of consensus does not...have a chance of being resolved by more or better arguments because the concept of species is itself a culturally constructed one". While I don't totally disagree, we still name species, we will still name species from this assemblage, and how we name species still matters. To sidestep the question (and reasonably so because it doesn't matter for their discussion) they fall back on Howell's use of Paleodemes to reflect "local populations of fossil taxa that are inferred to have shared a closer gene pool than their geographically and temporally more distant relative populations" (4).
